subtopics.title: what AI is
subtopics.teaching: Artificial intelligence is the design of computer systems that perform tasks requiring capabilities such as perception, prediction, language processing, planning or decision support.
subtopics.worked_example: A spam filter classifies messages using learned patterns; it does not need human-like consciousness to perform the task.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not equate fluent output with human understanding or consciousness.
subtopics.mastery: Define AI in terms of capabilities and distinguish an AI task from ordinary fixed automation.

subtopics.title: AI history
subtopics.teaching: AI research has passed through symbolic reasoning, expert systems, statistical machine learning, deep learning and today's foundation and generative models.
subtopics.worked_example: An expert system can be viewed as an earlier approach based on encoded rules, while a neural model learns patterns from examples.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not describe generative AI as if the field began only when chatbots became popular.
subtopics.mastery: Sequence major AI eras and explain how the dominant approach changed.

subtopics.title: machine learning concepts
subtopics.teaching: Machine learning enables a system to learn patterns from data so that its behaviour can generalize to new examples. Common learning settings include supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.
subtopics.worked_example: A model trained on labelled images of cats and dogs can learn to classify a new image it has not seen during training.
subtopics.pitfall: Memorizing training examples is not the same as learning a pattern that generalizes.
subtopics.mastery: Match a problem to an appropriate learning setting and explain training versus inference.

subtopics.title: models and data
subtopics.teaching: A model is a learned mathematical representation used to transform inputs into predictions, classifications, rankings or generated outputs. Data quality, representation and coverage strongly affect what the model can learn.
subtopics.worked_example: A handwriting classifier may fail on an unfamiliar script style if its training data contains only one narrow writing pattern.
subtopics.pitfall: A larger dataset does not automatically produce a better model if the data is noisy, biased or poorly labelled.
subtopics.mastery: Explain the relationship among data, model parameters, training and inference.

subtopics.title: AI applications
subtopics.teaching: AI is used in recommendation, search, translation, speech recognition, medical decision support, fraud detection, education and many other domains.
subtopics.worked_example: A learning platform can recommend practice topics from a student's previous performance while leaving the final learning decision to the student or teacher.
subtopics.pitfall: Calling every digital feature AI can hide whether a rule-based system or learned model is actually being used.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the AI component in a real application and state what input, output and decision it supports.

subtopics.title: data types
subtopics.teaching: Computing systems work with structured data such as tables and numerical values, semi-structured data such as JSON, and unstructured data such as images, audio and free text.
subtopics.worked_example: A student record may contain structured marks, while an uploaded essay is unstructured text that can be processed by language tools.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating all data as interchangeable can lead to unsuitable storage, preprocessing or modelling choices.
subtopics.mastery: Classify common data formats and explain why representation matters to an AI system.

subtopics.title: patterns
subtopics.teaching: Algorithms and models detect useful regularities such as frequency, correlation, sequence and similarity. A pattern is valuable only when it generalizes beyond the examples used to discover it.
subtopics.worked_example: A model may notice that certain words frequently occur in positive product reviews and use that pattern for sentiment classification.
subtopics.pitfall: A correlation in a dataset does not by itself prove that one factor causes another.
subtopics.mastery: Recognize meaningful patterns while distinguishing correlation, coincidence and causation.

subtopics.title: algorithms
subtopics.teaching: An algorithm is a finite, ordered procedure for solving a problem or transforming input into output. Good algorithmic thinking emphasizes clear steps, inputs, conditions, repetition and termination.
subtopics.worked_example: A binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search space rather than checking every item one by one.
subtopics.pitfall: A procedure that has no clear stopping condition or assumes an unsorted input without stating it is incomplete.
subtopics.mastery: Write or describe a stepwise algorithm and trace its behaviour on a small input.

subtopics.title: training data
subtopics.teaching: Training data provides examples from which a machine-learning model learns. Labels may be supplied by people or generated by a defined process, and representative coverage is critical.
subtopics.worked_example: If an image classifier is trained mostly on bright, front-facing photos, it may perform poorly on dark or side-view images.
subtopics.pitfall: More examples cannot fully correct a training set that systematically omits important cases.
subtopics.mastery: Explain how training examples influence model behaviour and identify gaps in a dataset.

subtopics.title: evaluation
subtopics.teaching: Model evaluation measures how well a system performs on data reserved for testing rather than merely showing performance on training examples. Metrics should match the task and its risks.
subtopics.worked_example: For a classifier, accuracy may be useful, while precision and recall can reveal different error patterns when false positives and false negatives have unequal costs.
subtopics.pitfall: A high training score alone is not evidence that a model generalizes well.
subtopics.mastery: Explain train/test separation and choose an evaluation measure appropriate to a stated task.

subtopics.title: text generation
subtopics.teaching: Text-generation systems produce sequences of tokens based on patterns learned from large language datasets. They can draft, summarize, transform and answer questions, but their output still requires verification.
subtopics.worked_example: A language model can turn bullet points into a structured explanation by predicting a plausible sequence of words.
subtopics.pitfall: Confident wording does not guarantee that a generated statement is factually correct.
subtopics.mastery: Describe how text generation works at a high level and identify when human verification is necessary.

subtopics.title: image generation
subtopics.teaching: Image-generation systems create images from learned representations of visual patterns, often conditioned on text or other inputs.
subtopics.worked_example: A text prompt describing a science laboratory can be transformed into a generated illustration whose visual details are synthesized by the model.
subtopics.pitfall: A generated image should not automatically be treated as a photograph or documentary evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish generated imagery from captured imagery and identify appropriate verification needs.

subtopics.title: multimodal systems
subtopics.teaching: Multimodal AI combines or coordinates information from different modalities such as text, images, audio and video so a system can reason or generate across them.
subtopics.worked_example: A model may inspect a chart image and answer a question about the labels while also using a written instruction.
subtopics.pitfall: Combining modalities does not guarantee that the system correctly understands every visual or audio detail.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the modalities involved in an AI task and explain why combining them can be useful.

subtopics.title: prompt concepts
subtopics.teaching: A prompt is an instruction or input that guides a generative model. Clear goals, relevant context, constraints, examples and an explicit output format can improve usefulness and consistency.
subtopics.worked_example: Instead of asking for 'a quiz', a prompt can specify the age group, topic, number of questions, difficulty and required answer format.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding unnecessary instructions or contradictory constraints can make an output less reliable.
subtopics.mastery: Construct a clear prompt with goal, context, constraints and expected output.

subtopics.title: limitations
subtopics.teaching: Generative AI can produce inaccurate claims, fabricated citations, incomplete reasoning, biased outputs or unsafe recommendations. Reliability depends on the task, input, model and verification process.
subtopics.worked_example: A student can use AI to draft practice questions but should check facts against authoritative study material before publishing them.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating a fluent response as automatically true is a major reliability error.
subtopics.mastery: List common generative-AI failure modes and select a verification strategy.

subtopics.title: sensors
subtopics.teaching: Sensors convert physical conditions such as light, temperature, distance, pressure or motion into measurable signals that a computing system can process.
subtopics.worked_example: A robot can use a distance sensor to estimate how close an obstacle is before deciding whether to move.
subtopics.pitfall: A sensor reading is a measurement with limitations and noise, not a perfect description of the environment.
subtopics.mastery: Explain the input role of sensors and identify how measurement errors can affect an automated system.

subtopics.title: actuators
subtopics.teaching: Actuators convert control signals into physical action, such as moving a motor, opening a valve or changing a robotic joint position.
subtopics.worked_example: A robot controller can command a motor to rotate a wheel after its sensors indicate that the path is clear.
subtopics.pitfall: Confusing sensing with actuation makes it difficult to reason about the control loop.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish sensors, controllers and actuators and trace information from measurement to action.

subtopics.title: control
subtopics.teaching: A control system repeatedly observes a state, compares it with a desired condition and changes an actuator command to influence the outcome. Feedback allows the system to correct deviations.
subtopics.worked_example: A smart fan can measure room temperature and adjust its speed to move toward a target temperature.
subtopics.pitfall: An open-loop action that never checks the result cannot automatically compensate for changing conditions.
subtopics.mastery: Describe a feedback loop using sensor input, controller decision and actuator output.

subtopics.title: autonomous systems
subtopics.teaching: An autonomous system can perceive its environment, make decisions according to programmed or learned policies and act with limited direct human control.
subtopics.worked_example: A warehouse robot can detect obstacles, plan a route and adjust movement while transporting an item.
subtopics.pitfall: Autonomous does not mean infallible or independent of human responsibility.
subtopics.mastery: Break an autonomous task into perception, decision and action stages and identify where human oversight may be needed.

subtopics.title: real-world automation
subtopics.teaching: Automation applies computing or control logic to repeatable physical or digital tasks, while intelligent automation may add perception, prediction or adaptive decision-making.
subtopics.worked_example: A warehouse can automatically route packages using barcode scans and conveyor controls, while an AI layer could predict congestion and adjust routing.
subtopics.pitfall: Automation and AI are not synonyms; a fixed rule can automate a task without machine learning.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish rule-based automation from AI-enabled automation and identify the control flow in a real system.

subtopics.title: hardware
subtopics.teaching: Computer hardware is the physical equipment used to sense, process, store or communicate information. Important components include processors, memory, storage devices, input/output devices and specialized accelerators.
subtopics.worked_example: A phone combines a processor, memory, storage, cameras and network hardware to run applications and communicate with other systems.
subtopics.pitfall: A faster processor alone does not guarantee a faster application; memory, storage, software and workload also matter.
subtopics.mastery: Identify major hardware components and explain their roles in an AI-enabled computing system.

subtopics.title: software
subtopics.teaching: Software is the set of programs and instructions that tell hardware what operations to perform. Operating systems, applications, libraries and drivers form different layers of software.
subtopics.worked_example: An operating system manages hardware resources while an AI application uses software libraries to load a model and process input.
subtopics.pitfall: Software is not the physical device itself, and installing more software does not increase hardware capacity.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish hardware from software and explain how software layers cooperate to deliver a computing task.

subtopics.title: networks
subtopics.teaching: A computer network connects devices so they can exchange data using defined communication protocols. Networks may be local or wide-area and can use wired or wireless links.
subtopics.worked_example: A student's browser can request a learning resource from a server over the internet using network protocols.
subtopics.pitfall: A network connection does not mean that every device or service is automatically trusted or secure.
subtopics.mastery: Explain the basic path of data between a client and service and identify the role of protocols.

subtopics.title: cloud concepts
subtopics.teaching: Cloud computing provides computing resources such as storage, servers, databases and processing through network-accessible infrastructure rather than requiring every resource to run locally.
subtopics.worked_example: An application can store large course files in cloud storage while a remote service performs processing when requested.
subtopics.pitfall: Cloud computing does not mean data has no physical location or that availability is guaranteed without limits.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish local computing from cloud services and identify common cloud resources.

subtopics.title: edge computing
subtopics.teaching: Edge computing places processing closer to where data is produced, reducing the need to send every input to a distant central service and potentially improving response time.
subtopics.worked_example: A factory camera can perform an initial safety check on an edge device and send only relevant events to a central system.
subtopics.pitfall: Edge processing does not automatically eliminate the need for networks, cloud services or security controls.
subtopics.mastery: Explain when edge processing can reduce latency and compare it with centralized processing.

subtopics.title: bias
subtopics.teaching: Algorithmic bias can arise when data, labels, model design, measurement or deployment conditions systematically produce poorer outcomes for some groups or situations.
subtopics.worked_example: A recognition system trained on a narrow population may perform differently when used with people whose characteristics were underrepresented in training data.
subtopics.pitfall: Bias is not limited to intentional discrimination; technical choices and incomplete data can also create unequal outcomes.
subtopics.mastery: Identify potential sources of bias in an AI pipeline and propose a way to investigate them.

subtopics.title: privacy
subtopics.teaching: Privacy concerns how personal information is collected, used, stored, shared and protected. AI systems can create additional risks when sensitive data is processed at scale or used for inference.
subtopics.worked_example: A learning application should collect only the student information needed for its stated function and restrict access to authorized users.
subtopics.pitfall: Data being technically available does not mean it is appropriate to collect or reuse for another purpose.
subtopics.mastery: Explain data minimization, purpose limitation and access control in an AI system.

subtopics.title: fairness
subtopics.teaching: Fairness in AI concerns whether system design and outcomes treat relevant people or groups appropriately according to the task and context. There is no single fairness rule for every application.
subtopics.worked_example: A scholarship screening system may need evaluation across relevant groups to check whether error rates differ materially.
subtopics.pitfall: Equal treatment at the input stage does not automatically guarantee equal outcomes after a model is deployed.
subtopics.mastery: Describe why fairness must be evaluated in context and identify evidence needed to assess an AI system.

subtopics.title: misinformation
subtopics.teaching: Misinformation is false or misleading information that can spread through human or automated systems. Generative tools can increase the speed and scale of producing convincing but inaccurate content.
subtopics.worked_example: An AI-generated post may combine a real photograph with a false claim about when or where it was taken.
subtopics.pitfall: Visual polish, confident language or many shares are not evidence that a claim is true.
subtopics.mastery: Apply source checking, cross-verification and provenance reasoning before accepting or sharing questionable AI-assisted content.

subtopics.title: human oversight
subtopics.teaching: Human oversight means people remain responsible for monitoring, reviewing or intervening in AI-assisted decisions when the consequences warrant it.
subtopics.worked_example: A teacher can review an AI-generated assessment report before using it to guide a student's learning plan.
subtopics.pitfall: Calling a system 'automated' does not transfer responsibility for consequential decisions to the machine.
subtopics.mastery: Identify where human review should occur in an AI workflow and explain what the reviewer must verify.

subtopics.title: IoT
subtopics.teaching: The Internet of Things connects physical objects equipped with sensors, processing and communication capabilities so they can collect, exchange or act on data.
subtopics.worked_example: A smart irrigation controller can use soil-moisture measurements and network connectivity to adjust watering.
subtopics.pitfall: An internet-connected device is not automatically secure or useful simply because it can transmit data.
subtopics.mastery: Describe the sensing, connectivity and action cycle of an IoT device.

subtopics.title: AR and VR
subtopics.teaching: Augmented reality overlays digital information on a user's view of the physical world, while virtual reality creates an immersive computer-generated environment.
subtopics.worked_example: An AR learning app can place labels over a real laboratory object, whereas a VR lesson can place the learner inside a simulated environment.
subtopics.pitfall: AR and VR are not interchangeable; their interaction models and hardware requirements differ.
subtopics.mastery: Compare AR and VR and select the appropriate technology for a stated learning or training scenario.

subtopics.title: quantum concepts
subtopics.teaching: Quantum computing uses quantum-mechanical phenomena to represent and manipulate information in ways that differ from classical bits. Qubits can exist in superposition and can be entangled.
subtopics.worked_example: A classical bit is represented as 0 or 1, while a qubit can be prepared in a quantum state involving amplitudes for both basis states.
subtopics.pitfall: A qubit being in superposition does not mean it simply stores every possible answer for free or that quantum computers are faster for every task.
subtopics.mastery: Explain bits versus qubits, superposition and entanglement at a conceptual level without treating them as magic speed multipliers.

subtopics.title: blockchain basics
subtopics.teaching: A blockchain is a distributed ledger in which records are grouped into blocks and linked using cryptographic mechanisms, with network rules governing how new records are accepted.
subtopics.worked_example: A blockchain network can maintain a shared transaction history across participating nodes without relying on one ordinary database server.
subtopics.pitfall: Blockchain does not make information automatically true, private or legally valid; the ledger records what the network accepts.
subtopics.mastery: Explain the shared-ledger concept and distinguish immutability claims from the accuracy of the original input.

subtopics.title: future technologies
subtopics.teaching: Emerging technologies should be evaluated by their capabilities, maturity, costs, risks, infrastructure requirements and likely applications rather than by novelty alone.
subtopics.worked_example: A new computing technology may be promising in research but still require years of engineering before it becomes practical at large scale.
subtopics.pitfall: A technology being described as 'next generation' is not evidence that it is ready for widespread deployment.
subtopics.mastery: Assess a proposed technology using evidence about readiness, benefit, limitations and risk.

subtopics.title: technology scenarios
subtopics.teaching: Technology reasoning starts by identifying the goal, users, inputs, constraints, outputs and risks before choosing a tool or architecture.
subtopics.worked_example: For an online learning service, a requirement for low-latency live interaction points toward real-time communication infrastructure rather than ordinary file storage alone.
subtopics.pitfall: Choosing a fashionable technology before defining the problem can create unnecessary complexity.
subtopics.mastery: Break a real-world technology scenario into requirements, constraints and candidate solution components.

subtopics.title: system design thinking
subtopics.teaching: System design organizes components and interfaces so a complete service can meet functional, performance, reliability, security and usability requirements.
subtopics.worked_example: A learning platform may separate authentication, application data, media storage and real-time communication because each has different responsibilities.
subtopics.pitfall: A system with many components is not automatically well designed; unnecessary coupling can make failures harder to isolate.
subtopics.mastery: Draw a simple component-level design and explain data flow, responsibilities and failure boundaries.

subtopics.title: AI problem solving
subtopics.teaching: AI problem solving involves defining the task, determining whether AI is appropriate, identifying data and evaluation criteria, selecting a method and planning validation and monitoring.
subtopics.worked_example: For classifying student questions, a team can first define the categories and success criteria before collecting representative examples and testing a model.
subtopics.pitfall: Starting with a model before defining the problem can produce impressive output that does not solve the intended task.
subtopics.mastery: Turn a real problem into an AI task specification with inputs, outputs, data, metric and validation plan.

subtopics.title: trade-offs
subtopics.teaching: Technology decisions involve trade-offs among accuracy, speed, cost, privacy, reliability, maintainability, energy use and user experience. Improving one dimension can sometimes worsen another.
subtopics.worked_example: Processing sensitive data locally may improve privacy but require more capable devices, while sending it to a server may simplify centralized processing but increase data-transfer concerns.
subtopics.pitfall: There is rarely one universally best technology independent of requirements.
subtopics.mastery: Compare at least two solution options using explicit criteria and justify the choice for a stated scenario.

subtopics.title: case analysis
subtopics.teaching: Case analysis evaluates a technology in its real context by combining requirements, evidence, system behaviour, benefits, limitations, risks and stakeholder impact.
subtopics.worked_example: A school considering an AI study assistant should evaluate accuracy, student privacy, teacher oversight, accessibility, cost and failure handling before adoption.
subtopics.pitfall: A case study based only on successful demonstrations can hide failure modes and operational costs.
subtopics.mastery: Analyze a technology case systematically and reach a justified recommendation supported by stated evidence.
